import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 341

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/341](https://www.erdosproblems.com/341)
* [Ben Green's Open Problem 7](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.1)
-/

open Nat Set Filter
open scoped Topology

namespace Erdos341

/--
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots < a_k\}$ be a finite set of integers and extend it to an infinite
sequence $\overline{A}=\{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ by defining $a_{n+1}$ for $n \geq k$ to be
the least integer exceeding $a_n$ which is not of the form $a_i + a_j$ with $i,j \leq n$.
Is it true that the sequence of differences $a_{m+1}-a_m$ is eventually periodic?

This problem is discussed under Problem 7 on Green's open problems list.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_341 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ (a : ℕ → ℤ),
        (∀ᶠ n in atTop,
          IsLeast { x | a n < x ∧ x ∉ { a i + a j | (i ≤ n) (j ≤ n) } } (a (n + 1))) →
        let d := fun i ↦ a (i + 1) - a i
        ∃ p > 0, ∀ᶠ m in atTop, d (m + p) = d m := by
  sorry

end Erdos341

reformulations.difference: The source starts with a finite, strictly ordered set of positive integers. Lean allows an arbitrary integer-valued sequence, including an unordered or repeated initial prefix, and imposes the greedy recurrence only eventually.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The eventual recurrence forces a strictly increasing integer tail, which is unbounded above. Choose a cutoff N in this tail such that a N is positive and exceeds every earlier value. Sort and deduplicate the positive values before N, then append a N, a (N+1), and so on. The resulting sequence b is strictly increasing and positive. At every subsequent step, all previous values are at most the current term, so a nonpositive summand cannot contribute to a forbidden sum exceeding that term. Sorting and deduplication also preserve the relevant sumset, since repeated summands are allowed. Thus b satisfies the same greedy recurrence and shares a fixed-index-shift tail with a; eventual periodicity of differences transfers between them. Conversely, every source extension satisfies Lean's hypothesis. This equivalence, including an explicit finite-seed cutoff formulation, is proved as Review341.statement_iff_explicit_positive_seed in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean, without any sorry dependency.

sources_consulted: Ben Green, 100 Open Problems, December 2025 update, §1, Problem 7 comments, p. 5: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf
